newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-VIALBE LEADS TEAM APOLOGY, WINS GOLD.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-VIALBE LEADS TEAM APOLOGY, WINS GOLD.

text.p: Yelena Vialbe made a public apology on behalf of Russia's team following the doping scandal at the Nordic skiing world championships before she won another gold medal on Thursday.
Vialbe, who completed the last lap for Russia in their expected triumph in the 4x5-km relay, has now won all four women's cross-country events.

But the winner of the 15-km and 10-km pursuit races could have lived without the gold in Sunday's 5-km race, which was awarded to her after fellow Russian Lyubov Yegorova was stripped of the title and disqualified on Wednesday for testing positive for the banned stimulant bromantan.

"It was a big shock and it was hard to find some sleep but we are top athletes and we did our best to win," said Vialbe, who picked up a Russian flag in the crowd in the finish straight and waved it until she crossed the line.
Before the start of the race, she took a microphone and addressed the spectators, saying the Russian team felt sorry but not responsible.

"The whole team wants to apologise to the public and the King (Harald of Norway) for what happened but you must understand that Lyubov Yegorova acted individually and that the team is not to blame," she said.
A few hours earlier, Yegorova, who was excluded from the championships, had left Trondheim discreetly in a car which headed for the Swedish border, witnesses said.

Alexander Grishun, head coach of the Russian women's team, said 30-year-old Yegorova, who won six Olympic golds and three world titles before this year's championships, was finished in the sport and had no chance of being picked for next year's Nagano Winter Olympics.
Vialbe and team mates Olga Danilova, Larissa Lasutina and Nina Gavrilyuk did not need Yegorova to outclass the opposition in the relay as they recorded a winning time of 56 minutes 40.20 seconds.

Norway, cheered on by some 20,000 enthusiasts lining the track, took the strongest start and led for over two laps. But with seven kilometres remaining, Gavrilyuk overtook Elin Nilsen to put Russia in front and she soon broke away.
The final lap was merely a formality for Vialbe, who came home 16 seconds ahead of Norwegian Trude Dybendahl-Hartz.
Finland won a close battle with Italy to take third place, 58.20 seconds behind the winners under bright sunshine.
The weather then changed dramatically and heavy snowfalls forced the organisers to put back the start of the ski jumping team competition by an hour.
It cleared up for Finland to retain their title with a brilliant second round in which all four jumpers went beyond 120 metres.

The Finnish squad, led by Janne Ahonen, who won the normal hill, individual event last Saturday, was second behind Japan after the first round but they fought back to score a winning total of 955.3 points.
Impressive jumping by Dieter Thoma, with the day's best mark at 129.5 metres followed by an effort at 120 metres, allowed Germany to take bronze with 845.6 points.
"I was the favourite in the normal hill competition and I didn't get a medal," said Thoma, who would have won gold on Saturday had he not fallen after landing in his second jump.
"It's nice to have a medal, let's hope I can get another one," he added, already thinking about next Saturday's high hill event.
Massive crowds are expected here on Friday for the men's relay in which Norway will start hot favourites.
